settings.title: Custom Orthotics for Flat Feet: How the NBA Assessment Shapes the Prescription

settings.editor: Not every flat foot needs an orthotic. How the assessment decides whether yours does, and what a custom device is actually designed to change.
DA Dr. Abbie Clinics clinical team 19 August 2026 · 4 min read
Book a session (opens online booking in a new tab) Call (02) 9545 4378

• A low arch is a shape, not automatically a problem. Many people with flat feet have no pain.
  • Flat feet matter when the way the foot rolls puts strain on tissue in the arch, heel, knee or hip.
  • A custom orthotic is made to a prescription from your assessment, not picked off a shelf.
  • Orthotics are one option among several and are only prescribed when the assessment shows they will change something.

“You have flat feet, you need orthotics” is advice a lot of people have been given. Sometimes it is right. Often it skips the most important step, which is working out whether the shape of your foot is actually causing the problem you came in with.

settings.title: Flat feet are not automatically a problem

settings.editor: Flat feet simply means the arch sits low, or flattens noticeably when you stand. It is common in both children and adults, and plenty of people with low arches never have any pain from them.

A low arch becomes relevant when the way the foot rolls through each step places strain somewhere that cannot tolerate it. That strain can show up in the arch or heel, but it can also appear further up, at the shin, the knee or the hip, because each step’s load travels up the leg.
The Najjarine Biomechanical Assessment was developed at Dr. Abbie Clinics and draws on engineering principles. For a flat foot, the questions it sets out to answer are practical ones:

• How does your foot and leg line up when you stand, and how does that change when you walk?
  • Where is the load going with each step, and which structure is being strained by it?
  • Does that strain match the pain you have come in with?
  • What are your shoes doing, and what does their wear pattern show?
The foot is assessed moving and under load, not only lying on a treatment table, because that is when the arch is doing its work. The findings are explained to you before anything is prescribed.

settings.title: What a custom orthotic is, and is not

settings.editor: An off-the-shelf insole is a generic shape designed to suit as many feet as possible. A custom orthotic is made to a prescription written from your own assessment, to change a specific problem that assessment identified.

The aim is not to force the foot into an idealised arch shape. It is to change the way load passes through the foot and up the leg, so the structure that has been overloaded is no longer taking the strain. That is why the prescription for two people with similar-looking flat feet can be quite different.
Our orthotics are manufactured on site at our Kirrawee head office rather than sent to an external laboratory.

settings.title: What to expect if orthotics are prescribed

settings.editor:
1. Assessment and prescription. The device is designed around what the assessment found, and around the shoes you actually wear. Bring them.
  2. Manufacture. The orthotic is made to that prescription. This usually takes around 7 to 10 days.
  3. Fitting. The device is fitted to your shoes and checked while you stand and walk.
  4. Settling in. There is usually a break-in period. Your podiatrist will tell you how to introduce them.
  5. Review. The fit and your symptoms are checked, and the device is adjusted if needed.

settings.title: When orthotics are not the answer

settings.editor: Orthotics are one of several treatments, not a default. If the assessment shows your flat feet are not the cause of your pain, there is nothing for an orthotic to fix. If they are part of the picture, other approaches may be used alongside or instead, including mobilisation, footwear changes or a strengthening programme.

Strapping is sometimes used first. If taping the foot a certain way relieves the pain, that tells us something useful about what an orthotic would need to do. For children, whose arches are still developing, the answer is often monitoring rather than a device.

settings.title: Questions worth asking at your appointment

settings.editor:
• Is my foot shape actually connected to my pain?
  • What would an orthotic change, specifically?
  • What else could we try, and why is this the better option for me?
  • Will it fit the shoes I wear most?
  • How will we know whether it is working?
A good answer to each should be possible after the assessment. If it is not, the prescription is a guess.
This article is general information, not a diagnosis. Everyone’s situation is different, so if you have pain or a concern about your feet or legs, have it assessed by a health professional.

image.alt: Dr Abbie Najjarine, Principal Podiatrist, Owner and Director at Dr. Abbie Clinics

settings.editor: About Abbie

Dr Abbie Najjarine (Podiatrist) is a podiatric biomechanical practitioner and lectures in his Najjarine Biomechanical Assessment (NBA) technique, the assessment behind every treatment plan at Dr. Abbie Clinics. He has been in private practice since 1990, treating patients with lower limb biomechanical dysfunction, which has given him extensive experience in the prescription and application of orthotic therapy.

Alongside his clinical work, Abbie has lectured extensively throughout Australia, New Zealand, the United Kingdom, Europe, Asia and Africa, teaching medical and allied health professionals lower limb biomechanical assessment and treatment techniques, joint mobilisation, prolotherapy, neural therapy, dry needling, strapping and physical therapy treatments.

He is the inventor of the Crown Medical orthotic, patented worldwide, invented the patented Footronics Football Kick Trainer, and is the author of The Orthotic Revolution and Clinical Biomechanics of the Lower Limb.

Abbie is the owner and Director of Dr. Abbie Clinics, and has been Director of AOL Footcare Centre since 1993. He was Director and Founder of the International College of Biomechanics from 1996 to 2019, Director of ICB Medical from 2000 to 2019 and of ICB Gait and Posture Clinics from 2003 to 2019, and a board member of the Australian Podiatry Association (NSW & ACT) from 2010 to 2013.

settings.editor: What it is
A fine needle is placed into a trigger point in the muscle or fascia. Nothing is injected — the needle itself is the treatment, used to release tissue that has become restrictive.
People with tight or restricted soft tissue in the calf, foot or lower leg that is contributing to how they load and where they hurt.
Where it is available

image.alt: Dry needling being applied to a patient’s lower leg

settings.editor: In detail
Muscles, tendons and ligaments can develop tight, taut bands: trigger points, scar tissue or adhesions. These limit how far and how smoothly a joint moves, and cause pain.

image.alt: Fine needles placed in a muscle

settings.editor: 01
A fine acupuncture needle is placed in or around the taut band. It can cause a small twitch in the muscle.
02
The body treats the needle as a foreign object, like a splinter or bee sting. It releases histamine and increases blood flow, bringing in the cells responsible for repair.
03
The needle also stimulates sensory nerve fibres that help turn down the pain messages reaching the brain.
04
Most often the calves, the ITB and around the knees, usually alongside orthotics so the tight muscle is not working against the correction.
How it works here
Dry Needling is prescribed against a diagnosis, never against a symptom. That is what the Najjarine Biomechanical Assessment is for.

image.alt: Dr Abbie Najjarine assessing a patient’s gait on a treadmill

settings.editor: 01
The assessment identifies which tissue is restricted and whether that restriction is part of what is causing your pain.
02
Needles are placed into the trigger points and left briefly. Most people feel a dull ache or a twitch rather than a sharp pain.
03
Needling is normally combined with mobilisation, stretching or orthotic therapy so the tissue does not simply tighten again.

image.alt: Dr Abbie Najjarine demonstrating a lower limb assessment, with alignment marked on the leg and practitioners observing

Questions

settings.title: Is dry needling the same as acupuncture?

settings.editor: They use similar needles but not the same reasoning. Dry needling targets specific trigger points identified in your assessment.
Most people describe a dull ache or a brief twitch rather than a sharp pain. Tell your podiatrist during the session if it is uncomfortable.
No. Nothing is injected in dry needling — the needle itself is the treatment. Injectable treatment is a separate service, Injection Therapy.
Some people feel mild soreness for a day, similar to after exercise. Your podiatrist will tell you what to expect for your case.

settings.title: How many sessions will I need?

settings.editor: It depends on what the assessment found. Your podiatrist will set that out before you commit to a course.
